Incircles and Circumcircles

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: Drag the corners of a triangle and see where the centers of three circles land.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the circles and press Check the theorem.
Look for the math

Move a corner of the triangle and the three small circles change size, but their centers stay on one and the same big circle. That is the droodle on Bogomolny's page: a fact you can watch survive every drag.

The incenter and its circle

The three angle bisectors of triangle ABC meet at one point I, the incenter. It is equally far from all three sides, so a circle centered at I can touch each side. The applet builds that incircle by averaging its three distances to the sides; the logic test checks that this equals area divided by the semiperimeter on every triangle tried.

Where the three centers go

Each small circle is the circumcircle of I and two corners: for instance (IBC). Its center O_A lies on the big circle through A, B and C, and also on the bisector from A. In fact O_A is the second place that bisector meets the big circle. The test verifies all three centers this way, then presses the same check on more than a thousand triangles: acute, right, obtuse, mirrored and very flat. All pass.

Why the centers land there

Let M_a, M_b, M_c be the midpoints of BC, IC and IB. The lines from O_A to those midpoints are perpendicular to the sides they bisect, so the page's angle equations hold: ∠M_a O_A M_c = ∠IBC = B/2 and ∠M_a O_A M_b = ∠ICB = C/2. Adding them gives ∠B O_A C = B + C, or ∠B O_A C + A = 180°, which is exactly the test for a point on the circumcircle of ABC. The logic test measures each of those angles, not just the final on-circle distance.

Johnson's version, and a source note

The page adds that O_A is the midpoint of arc BC and that the circle centered there with radius DB = DC passes through I: the test confirms DB = DC = DI. It also mentions a weaker 1988 Olympiad problem asking that the circles (ABC) and (O_A O_B O_C) be concentric. That holds here too, and more strongly the two circles coincide, because all three centers already lie on (ABC).

The live cut-the-knot page now shows a GeoGebra drawing rather than the Java applet. The applet and its checkboxes were recovered from a 2006 Wayback capture, and this port follows that applet: the same three toggles, the same draggable corners and the same drawn circles.

Try a long, thin triangle: some centers fly far outside the picture, yet Check the theorem still finds them on the big circle.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
